lead: Storage virtualization hides many physical disks behind logical volumes. Network virtualization hides physical links behind virtual NICs and switches. Both let a hypervisor give each VM a clean, isolated device while sharing hardware. A VM sees a disk that may span arrays, or a network card that may share one uplink with dozens of neighbours. Cloud providers use these layers to sell storage and bandwidth in slices, to snapshot and migrate VMs, and to keep tenants apart. The same ideas support a Chennai firm renting IaaS capacity without buying a disk per server.
prereq: You need: 3.5 for device virtualization and 3.1 for isolation.

blocks.text: Physical disks differ in size, speed and failure rate. A storage pool hides that variety. The pool groups disks and lets an administrator carve logical volumes from one free-capacity number. A LUN (logical unit number) is the identifier of a logical disk presented to a host. The hypervisor gives each VM a virtual disk; that virtual disk is a file or volume inside the pool. The VM sees a normal block device and does not know which physical disks hold its blocks.
RAID 5 is common inside a pool. It stripes blocks across disks and stores parity. A hot spare lowers usable capacity.
Usable RAID 5 U = (n − 1) × d; P = Σ v<sub>i</sub>; overprovision = P ÷ U
blocks.where: n is number of equal disks; d is TB per disk; v<sub>i</sub> are thin volume sizes in TB; P is total provisioned logical TB; U is usable pool TB.

blocks.text: Thin provisioning sells logical size before physical blocks exist. A thin volume of 1.5 TB is created at once, but blocks are allocated on first write. Total logical P is the sum of all volume sizes. A ratio above 1 means promises exceed physical space; writes fail when the pool fills. Snapshots record a point-in-time view, usually by copy-on-write: old blocks are kept when new writes arrive. A snapshot protects against a bad update, not against loss of the whole pool.

Network virtualization gives each VM its own vNIC (virtual network interface card). The vNIC has a MAC address and driver inside the guest, but it is software. Frames leave the vNIC and enter a virtual switch (vSwitch), a layer-2 switch running in the hypervisor or host. The vSwitch forwards frames between vNICs and out through a physical NIC. It can apply policy: VLAN tag, bandwidth cap, or security rule. Traffic between two VMs on the same vSwitch can stay on the host and never touch the physical NIC.

VLAN (virtual LAN) adds a 12-bit tag to Ethernet frames and keeps groups in separate broadcast domains. It isolates traffic; it does not encrypt it. VXLAN wraps Ethernet frames inside UDP/IP and uses a 24-bit VNI (VXLAN network identifier). That carries layer-2 networks over a routed layer-3 data-centre fabric, beyond the 4094 usable VLAN IDs.

SDN (software-defined networking) separates the control plane from the data plane. The control plane decides paths; the data plane forwards packets. A controller programs flow rules into vSwitches and physical switches. The physical link becomes a shared resource; virtual links are policy. If twenty VMs each have a 1 Gb/s cap and share one 10 Gb/s uplink, demand is 20 Gb/s and contention is 20 ÷ 10 = 2:1. A cap does not reserve bandwidth.

The VM never sees the physical path. Its disk driver writes to a virtual disk. The hypervisor maps that disk to a volume in the storage pool. The pool maps blocks to physical disks and applies RAID. Its network driver sends frames to a vNIC. The vNIC is attached to a vSwitch port. The vSwitch maps the port to a VLAN or VXLAN segment and chooses an uplink physical NIC. This chain is why live migration works: if both hosts can reach the same storage pool and the same virtual network, the VM's disk and MAC address move with it. The figure shows both chains, one for storage and one for network. Some syllabi call this pair storage and network virtualization and link it to software-defined networks.

figure.caption: A VM reaches a virtual disk, storage pool and physical disks, and separately a vNIC, virtual switch and physical NIC. Notice that the VM touches only virtual devices.

spec.title: Virtual disk and virtual NIC
spec.aria: A virtual machine connects down to a virtual disk, then a storage pool and physical disks; it also connects to a vNIC, a virtual switch and a physical NIC.

examples.question: A storage pool has 6 disks of 2 TB each in RAID 5. Twelve VMs each receive a thin volume of 1.5 TB. Average real use is 40% of provisioned logical capacity. Twenty VMs each have a 1 Gb/s vNIC cap and share one 10 Gb/s uplink. Find usable pool capacity, total provisioned capacity, overprovision ratio, real data, spare usable capacity, network demand and contention ratio.
steps: Usable RAID 5 capacity = (6 − 1) × 2 TB = 5 × 2 TB = 10 TB.
Real data at 40% use = 0.40 × 18 TB = 7.2 TB.
Spare usable capacity = 10 TB − 7.2 TB = 2.8 TB, so the data fits.
examples.answer: Usable capacity is 10 TB, provisioned capacity is 18 TB, overprovision ratio is 1.8, real data is 7.2 TB with 2.8 TB spare; network demand is 20 Gb/s on a 10 Gb/s uplink, contention 2:1.
examples.check:
n = 6
d = 2.0
usable = (n - 1) * d
vms = 12
vol = 1.5
prov = vms * vol
over = prov / usable
real = 0.40 * prov
spare = usable - real
vm_links = 20
cap = 1.0
uplink = 10.0
demand = vm_links * cap
cont = demand / uplink
for x in (usable, prov, over, real, spare, demand, cont):
    print(f'{x:g}')

traps: Thin provisioning does not guarantee space. An overprovision ratio above 1 can fail when the pool fills.
A VLAN isolates broadcast domains but does not encrypt frames; it is not a confidentiality control.
RAID 5 usable capacity is (n − 1) × d, not n × d. Parity consumes one disk's worth.
A snapshot is a point-in-time view in the same pool, not an independent backup; pool loss loses both.
A vNIC bandwidth cap limits a VM but does not reserve uplink bandwidth; the sum of caps can exceed the physical link.

quiz.a: A LUN is a logical unit number, an identifier for a logical disk presented to a host. A storage pool is a group of physical disks whose capacity is carved into logical volumes.

quiz.q: Why does thin provisioning need capacity monitoring?
quiz.a: It promises logical size before physical blocks exist. If many volumes are written at once, the pool can run out and writes fail; monitoring tracks real use against usable capacity.

quiz.q: A pool has 8 disks of 4 TB in RAID 5. Twenty VMs get 2 TB thin volumes. Average use is 50% of provisioned capacity. Find usable capacity, provisioned capacity, overprovision ratio and real data.
quiz.a: Usable = (8 − 1) × 4 TB = 28 TB. Provisioned = 20 × 2 TB = 40 TB. Overprovision = 40 ÷ 28 ≈ 1.43. Real data = 0.50 × 40 TB = 20 TB, which fits in 28 TB with 8 TB spare.

quiz.q: Thirty VMs each have a 2 Gb/s cap and share a 10 Gb/s uplink. Find network demand and contention ratio.
A VLAN keeps two tenants apart. Does it stop a sniffing attack on the physical uplink? Explain.
quiz.a: No. VLAN tags separate broadcast domains but frames stay readable; a compromised switch or trunk port can copy them. Encryption such as IPsec or TLS is needed for secrecy.

quiz.q: What does SDN separate, and how does a controller change a vSwitch?
quiz.a: It separates the control plane (path decision) from the data plane (forwarding). A controller installs flow rules in the vSwitch so packets match and forward without a controller call for every packet.

quiz.q: Why can a VM live-migrate only if both hosts share a storage pool and a virtual network?
quiz.a: The VM's disk must exist at the destination, so the same pool or a replicated volume is needed. Its MAC and vSwitch port must also exist on the destination virtual network; otherwise the disk and network connections break.

beyond: Not for the exam. In cloud platforms, storage pools are often software-defined and network overlays are managed by SDN controllers; Ceph and Open vSwitch are common open-source building blocks. Researchers study erasure coding to cut RAID overhead and programmable NICs to move virtual switching into hardware. Search terms: thin provisioning overcommit, VXLAN VNI, OpenFlow, software-defined storage.
